title: Grammars, parse trees and pushdown automata
subtitle: Add one stack to a finite automaton and it can count and match brackets — exactly the power of a grammar.

sections.title: Context-free grammars
sections.body: A context-free grammar has variables (S, E…), terminals (a, b, +…), productions A → α, and a start variable. A string is in the language if the start variable can be rewritten into it. The grammar S → aSb | ab generates aⁿbⁿ — the language no finite automaton can recognise. Deriving aaabbb: S => aSb => aaSbb => aaabbb.

questions.prompt: Which language does S → aSb | ab generate?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each use of aSb adds one a on the left and one b on the right.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — deriving aaabbb
figures.note: Each step rewrites the leftmost variable; the last frame adds the parse tree.

sections.title: Parse trees and ambiguity
sections.body: A parse tree shows which productions built a string. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees — a real problem for compilers, because the tree is the meaning. The classic fix is to encode precedence in layers of variables: E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → (E) | a. Then a+a*a has exactly one tree, with * binding tighter than +.

choices.text: Some string has more than one parse tree.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Different trees can mean different values.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — unambiguous expression grammar
figures.note: The tree shows the multiplication grouped under the addition.
figures.script: var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"g2","engine":"cfg","grammar":"E -> E+T | T\nT -> T*F | F\nF -> (E) | a","string":"a+a*a","width":600,"height":440});

g2.derivation: E => E+T => T+T => F+T => a+T => a+T*F => a+F*F => a+a*F => a+a*a

sections.title: Simplification and normal forms
sections.body: Before analysis, remove useless variables, ε-productions and unit productions (A → B). Chomsky normal form allows only A → BC and A → a; Greibach normal form only A → aα. Any CFL (without ε) has grammars in both forms. BNF is the notation compilers use for language syntax.

worked.why: Convert S → aSb | ab to Chomsky normal form.
Introduce A → a, B → b and split: S → AC | AB, C → SB.
worked.math: S\to AC\mid AB,\ C\to SB,\ A\to a,\ B\to b

questions.prompt: A production allowed in Chomsky normal form is…

choices.text: A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal).

sections.title: Pushdown automata
sections.body: A PDA is an NFA with a stack. A move depends on the state, the input symbol (or ε) and the top of the stack, and changes the state and replaces the top with a string. To recognise aⁿbⁿ: push an A for every a, pop one for every b, accept if the stack returns to its bottom marker Z. Watch the stack on the right.

questions.prompt: What lets a PDA check aⁿbⁿ but not a DFA?

choices.text: The stack stores an unbounded count of a’s.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Finite states cannot count without bound.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Its memory grows with the input.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That would be a Turing machine.

figures.note: Top of the stack is the highlighted cell.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.2 — aabbb is rejected
figures.note: One b too many: the stack runs dry.

problems.prompt: Does the PDA in the figure accept aabbb?
problems.answer: No. After aa, two A’s are pushed; the first two b’s pop them; the third b finds only Z on the stack, so no move is possible: rejected.

sections.title: CFG ⇔ PDA, closure and limits
sections.body: Context-free languages are exactly those accepted by PDAs: a grammar becomes a PDA that guesses derivations on its stack, and a PDA becomes a grammar whose variables stand for “go from state p to q popping this symbol”. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, but not under intersection or complement. The pumping lemma for CFLs (pump two places at once) shows aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free. Context-sensitive grammars (α → β with |α| ≤ |β|) sit one level above.

choices.text: No — one stack can match two counts but not three.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The CFL pumping lemma proves it.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• CFG generates, PDA recognises: same class.
  • Ambiguity lives in the grammar; layering operators removes it.
  • CNF: A → BC | a.
